assessments.task_description:
Active engagement is required for all scheduled workshop classes in Weeks 1, 2, 4, 8 and 13. During these workshops, students will undertake research and/or develop relevant information that will be analysed, interpreted and synthesised according to the specific requirements outlined in class. These activities are designed to support students in demonstrating practical research skills, effective data synthesis, and meaningful engagement with relevant research literature.

In each workshop, students will undertake research activities connected to the relevant learning module. Foundational guidance on data collection and analysis will be provided. Students will then examine their data in relation to the research question developed during the Week 1 workshop. This will require students to prepare suitable visualisations, tables or other formats to communicate their findings to the class.

Students will also be expected to engage with relevant scholarly literature and connect their findings to existing knowledge in the field. This will involve critically analysing the literature to show an understanding of the methods used in the workshops, as well as explaining how the research question or goal relates to the broader discipline.


Use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) 

This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance.

A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.

To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools.

assessments.task_description:
Students are required to develop, present and record a conference-style research presentation. The presentation must be presented as 8 to 10 minute recorded presentation and be easy to understand for a generalist sport science audience.


The presentation must include the following sections: Introduction, Methods, Results, Practical Applications, Conclusion and References.


Conference-Style Research Presentation topics will be determined during the Week 1 Workshop.


Broad focus areas for your Conference-Style Research Presentation and associated research project (choose one from the list):

a)      Strength training in a Periodised Plan for Elite Athletes

b)      Power training in a Periodised Plan for Elite Athletes

c)      Speed training in a Periodised Plan for Elite Athletes

d)      Agility training in a Periodised Plan for Elite Athletes

e)      Endurance training in a Periodised Plan for Elite Athletes

f)       Tapering for peak performance in a Periodised Plan for Elite Athletes

g)      Athlete Monitoring in a Periodised Plan for Elite Athletes

h)      Novel Skill Acquisition in a Periodised Plan for Elite Sport

i)        Training Elite Paralympic Athletes using a Periodise Plan


Please note: Elite athletes are athletes who have achieved a recognised level of competitive success at the highest levels of their sport, typically demonstrated through selection, ranking, representation, or performance outcomes. This may include athletes competing at national, international, professional, Olympic, Paralympic, or world championship level. The term generally refers to an athlete’s current or demonstrated status within the upper tier of competition. High performance athletes, by contrast, are athletes who are engaged in structured, intensive training and development systems designed to optimise performance and support progression toward elite competition. They may be highly skilled and committed, but they may not yet have achieved elite-level selection, ranking, or competitive outcomes. The term often refers to the performance environment, training pathway, and developmental intent rather than confirmed elite status. In conducting the research for your project, please first attempt to net study who have examined Elite Athletes and then if you need to expand your search you can include High Performance Athletes. Please do not search for Recreational Athletes as defined by individuals who engage in sport or structured physical activity for personal, social, health, or enjoyment-related reasons, rather than as part of an elite or high-performance sporting pathway.

 

Background to the task

Students are required to complete a systematised review on their chosen topic area. A systematised review uses selected features of a systematic review, such as a clearly defined research question, structured search strategy, transparent inclusion and exclusion criteria, and a summary of relevant evidence. However, unlike a full systematic review, a systematised review is smaller in scope and does not require students to complete every stage of a formal systematic review, such as exhaustive database searching, duplicate independent screening, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or meta-analysis. A systematised review is also different from a scoping review, which is usually designed to map the breadth, range and nature of evidence across a broad topic area rather than answer a focused question about a specific intervention, training approach or outcome. For this assessment, students should use their systematised review to identify, organise and synthesise relevant research evidence that directly informs their selected poster topic and supports clear practical applications for elite or high-performance sport.

 

For the purposes of this assessment, students are restricted to using one academic database to complete their systematised review. This requirement is intended to ensure that the review remains achievable within the scope of the course while still allowing students to demonstrate a structured and transparent approach to searching, screening and synthesising relevant literature. Students must clearly identify the database used, justify its relevance to their chosen topic, and report the search terms, filters, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and screening process applied. Although a full systematic review would usually require searching multiple databases, this assessment only requires students to conduct a focused search within one database and present the most relevant evidence in a clear and methodologically transparent way.

 

Students must use Covidence to manage the article screening process for their systematised review. After completing their search in the selected academic database, students should export their search results and upload them into Covidence for screening. Students are then required to screen articles by title and abstract against their inclusion and exclusion criteria, before progressing eligible articles to full-text screening where final decisions about inclusion are made. The screening process must be clearly documented in the Methods section of the poster, including the number of articles identified, screened, excluded and included in the final review. Access to Covidence is available through the UQ Library website and is free for UQ students when accessed through the University of Queensland institutional licence. Students should use their UQ username/email to request access via the UQ Library Covidence page before commencing their review.

 

Students must use the PICO framework to guide the development and completion of their systematised review. PICO should be used to clearly define the research question and structure the search strategy by identifying the Population, Intervention, Comparison and Outcome relevant to the selected topic area. Students should demonstrate how each element of PICO informed their literature search, including the selection of keywords, search terms, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the overall scope of the review. The PICO framework should also be used to support the organisation and interpretation of evidence presented in the poster, ensuring that the review remains focused, systematic and aligned with the chosen research question. Students are expected to report their PICO framework clearly within the Methods section of the presentation.

 

Students must complete a quality appraisal of the articles included in their systematised review using the relevant Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Tool. The selected JBI tool must match the study design of each included article, such as qualitative research, randomised controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, cohort studies, cross-sectional studies or systematic reviews. Students should use the JBI tool to assess the methodological quality, rigour and trustworthiness of each included study, and briefly summarise the appraisal outcomes in the Methods and/or Results section of their presentation. The quality appraisal should not simply determine whether an article is included or excluded; rather, it should help students interpret the strength and limitations of the evidence and support more balanced conclusions and practical applications. Students should clearly identify which JBI tool was used and explain how the appraisal informed their interpretation of the literature.


Students must clearly describe, in the Conference-Style Research Presentation, the translation of their research when implemented as part of a periodised training program in sport. They must justify why their research would be implemented as part of an elite athlete training program and recommendations about how this would occur as part of this periodised plan. Consideration should be given to testing as part of this implementation strategy. 

 

Presentation Requirements:

  • Students must record their presentation as an individual for between 8 to 10 minutes. Any content extending beyond 10 minutes will not be assessed.
  • Students can use a slide show to aid their presentation.
  • Students are discouraged from relying on notes during their presentation.
  • Students may use slides but should limit reliance on notes
  • Students are to record their presentation using video software such as Zoom or Microsoft Teams.
  • The students' face must be clearly visible with high quality sound. In view, must be your face along with the respective slide projection.
  • No additional electronic media, such as sound or video files, are permitted beyond the recording.
  • No additional props, such as costumes, laboratory equipment, musical instruments or similar items, are allowed.


This assessment task must be completed as a recorded presentation and submitted through the relevant online Learn.UQ assignment submission link.


This is your opportunity to demonstrate your ability to synthesise knowledge, justify practice, and communicate with clarity and confidence—essential skills for professionals working with high-performance athletes. Presentations must clearly describe the conclusions, outcomes and impact of research when implemented as part of a periodised training program in sport

Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance.

A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.

assessments.task_description:
The Final Examination will give you the chance to showcase everything you’ve learned across the semester.

You’ll have 120 minutes to complete 80 multiple-choice questions and 1 extended answer question all designed to assess your understanding of key concepts, critical thinking, and application of theory to practice.

The exam will draw on material covered from Weeks 1 to 13, including lectures, readings, and workshop activities available through Learn.UQ. This is your opportunity to demonstrate your growth, insight, and readiness to apply your knowledge in real-world professional contexts.

Use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) 

This assessment task is to be completed in-person. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.

learning_activities.topic:
RESEARCHING WITH A PLAN IN SPORT AND STRENGTH AND POWER TRAINING

Get ready to unleash explosive performance! In this week’s workshop, you’ll dive into the art and science of strength and power periodisation—exploring how to strategically plan and progress training to maximise force, speed, and athletic output. You’ll break down real-world examples, apply evidence-based methods, and develop your own periodised models designed to elevate athlete performance to the next level.

ANALYSIS OF LITERATURE IN ELITE SPORT AS WELL AS SPEED, AGILITY AND ENDURANCE

Shift gears and accelerate performance! This week focuses on the science and strategy behind speed and agility periodisation. You’ll explore how to structure training phases that build explosive acceleration, sharp change of direction, and game-changing agility. You’ll learn how to tailor speed-focused programs that meet the demands of elite sport and keep athletes moving at their peak, all season long.

learning_activities.topic:
NAVIGATING THE RESEARCH ENVIRONMENT IN SPORT AND PERIODISATION FOR MAXIMUM PERFORMANCE

Train smart, perform sharper! This week, you'll unlock the keys to managing training load for peak performance. You’ll explore how to balance stress and recovery, avoid overtraining, and fine-tune athlete readiness using monitoring tools and load management strategies. Learn how to optimise performance by making data-informed decisions that keep athletes progressing, adapting, and performing at their best when it matters most.

FRAMEWORKS RELEVANT TO SPORT RESEARCH AND TAPERING FOR PEAK PERFORMANCE

Finish strong with precision! This week explores the power of tapering—the strategic reduction of training load to unleash peak performance at the right moment. You’ll learn how to design tapering strategies that maintain fitness, reduce fatigue, and optimise physiological and psychological readiness. Discover how elite athletes time their best performances through well-executed taper plans that bring it all together when it counts most.

ANALYSING THE FINDINGS OF SPORT RESEARCH AND ATHLETE MONITORING

Unlock elite potential! This week, you'll dive into the integrated strategies that drive optimal athletic performance across the season. You’ll explore how to align long-term development frameworks with cutting-edge monitoring practices to enhance athlete progression, resilience, and results. From training adjustments to performance tracking, you’ll learn how to make smart, data-driven decisions that support sustainable success at the highest level.

See the science come to life! This week brings periodised training models into real-world focus. You’ll analyse how elite teams and athletes structure their seasons using tailored, adaptive plans that respond to the evolving demands of competition. Through case studies and applied examples, you’ll gain practical insight into how periodisation is implemented across different sports to maximise performance, manage fatigue, and maintain competitive edge.

Plan the path to podium performance! In this week, you’ll master the art of annual training planning and periodisation. Learn tools to map out a full season of training that strategically balances progression, performance, and recovery. You’ll explore how to structure macro-, meso-, and micro-cycles to align with competition calendars, developmental stages, and performance goals—giving athletes the best chance to peak at the right time.
